FYPFinal-year project

Design and Experimental Evaluation of a Low-Cost Ultrasonic-Based 2D Occupancy Mapping System · 63-page dissertation, supervised by Bilal Alhawaisil · BEng (Hons), June 2026

Can one £3 ultrasonic sensor build a credible map?

Autonomous mapping normally needs LiDAR and a full SLAM stack. I built a differential-drive rover for under £50 with a single HC-SR04 on a servo, then tested honestly where it works and where it breaks: sensor, odometry, map, path following and navigation, each measured against published benchmarks.

Architecture: PC as brain

BrainMATLAB host: odometry, Bayesian log-odds grid with Bresenham ray-casting, Stanley path following and A* planning with obstacle inflation. 33 Hz control loop, 5 Hz UI.
BridgeESP8266 as a transparent, low-latency Wi-Fi UDP relay.
ControllerArduino Nano: motor control, encoder interrupts and the servo-mounted sensor head, streaming telemetry at about 33 Hz.

The honest finding

Specular reflection is the limit. Past 30° incidence the echo starts to vanish, which forced a scan-before-plan behaviour. Both failed missions were fail-safe: a single spurious reading created a phantom obstacle, so the rover stopped rather than collided.

Contribution and next steps

Integrating probabilistic mapping, closed-loop following and graph-based planning on an ultrasonic-only platform, plus an honest characterisation of where it fails. I also adapted an Ackermann-derived Stanley controller to differential drive. Next: overhead-webcam loop closure and quadrature encoders to cut dead-reckoning drift.
